title: Building an AI-Driven Production Pipeline for a Ten-Property Creative Department of One
summary: I was the sole creative director for a ten-property luxury hospitality portfolio, drowning in repetitive production work. I designed a two-layer AI system — Claude for direction, Claude Code for execution — that turned one-off design requests into a repeatable, reviewable pipeline.
bodyHtml:
The problem

I run creative production for the Soroi Collection — ten open luxury safari and coastal properties across Kenya, an eleventh opening in 2027, all needing brand-consistent factsheets, social content, guest-facing guides, menus, brochures, and print collateral. I'm the only person doing it.

The bottleneck was never creative judgment. It was the overhead around it. Every request meant re-locating the right image out of 31,000+ files scattered across an external drive with years of inconsistent filing. Every document meant re-stating the same rate figures, room counts, and brand rules from memory, because the source of truth lived in PDFs and spreadsheets nobody had reconciled. Every property had its own brand quirks — some confirmed, some not — with no single place recording which was which. And the actual "design work" — populating templates, checking numbers, fixing formatting — was consuming the hours that should have gone to the work only I could do: creative direction, art direction, final polish.

This is the shape of a problem a lot of production teams have, not just creative ones: a huge amount of an expert's time is going into work that's necessary but not actually where their expertise adds value. The question I set out to answer was whether an AI system could absorb the repeatable part of that work reliably enough that I could trust it, without me having to babysit every step.

What I did

Splitting the system into two roles that match how the work actually happens. Rather than trying to build one tool that does everything, I split the system along a real seam: a directing layer and an execution layer. Claude, used conversationally, holds the full context — property facts, brand rules, contacts, rate documents, past decisions — and is where I think through a brief, draft copy, and make judgment calls. Claude Code is where that judgment gets executed: reading files, running scripts, calling Canva's API, touching the actual asset drive. The handoff between the two is a structured JSON brief — a deliberately boring, versionable artifact rather than a vague instruction, so nothing gets lost in translation between "what I decided" and "what gets built."

A locked production pipeline instead of one-off generation. Every output — a factsheet, a social post, a brochure — follows the same sequence: brand-consistent HTML/CSS design, converted to PDF via a headless Chromium pipeline, imported into Canva as the fixed visual layer, then populated with real content through Canva's API using a deterministic field-naming convention ({property}_{section}_{field}_{index}). The important decision here was negative: never let the AI generate visuals directly inside Canva. Canva's native AI generation is fast but uncontrollable at the level of brand precision this needs. Locking the visual design in HTML first, and treating Canva purely as the population and client-facing polish layer, meant every output inherited the same font, spacing, and color system by construction, not by hoping the model got it right each time.

Indexing the mess instead of trying to fix it. 31,000+ images and years of Google Drive drift weren't going to get manually reorganized — that's a multi-month project with no clear payoff. Instead I built a search-index model: index by file content rather than filename (so years of bad labeling didn't propagate into the new system), and link out to the source of truth rather than migrating anything. The win was making the existing chaos searchable and usable, not making it disappear.

Designing for the model's actual failure modes, not its ideal behavior. Two decisions came directly from watching where things went wrong. First: the system never marks a task complete until the output physically exists in a pending-review/ folder, and nothing moves to approved/ without my sign-off — the system produces drafts, not final decisions, on purpose. Second: I had it label its own outputs at the sentence level — [Inference], [Speculation], [Unverified] — because at launch, half the brand rules genuinely didn't exist yet (several properties had no confirmed hex codes or fonts). A system that guesses convincingly in that gap is worse than one that flags it. Making the system surface what it didn't know, instead of filling the silence, was one of the more important calls I made.

Working around real platform constraints rather than designing around an idealized API. Canva's editing API can't create new elements or change fonts, and stripping and repopulating a text block silently loses inline bold formatting. Rather than let those limits cause quiet corruption, I built the workflow to detect and flag exactly what the API can't safely touch, so those become known 30-second manual fixes instead of invisible defects.

The result

The system now runs real production, not a demo. Concretely: 31,809 images indexed off the primary asset drive, with 761 misfiled room images corrected as a direct output of the audit. A 165-slide, ~107MB sales presentation was processed to extract and organize 278 usable photographs into per-property folders, filtering out roughly 500 tiny mask and gradient fragments automatically — work that would otherwise have been an afternoon of manual clicking. Full 18-page guest-facing documents have been audited against source-of-truth rate sheets and corrected directly in the live design rather than via a marked-up copy. An illustrated map-generation pipeline was debugged and fixed at the root — image-conditioned prompting instead of text-only — so the fix applies to the whole ten-property series, not just one map.

None of this replaced my judgment. It replaced the hours I was spending before I could apply it — finding the right file, checking a number against the right source, re-keying a correction by hand. The system is deliberately unglamorous: JSON briefs, folder conventions, a human approval gate that can't be skipped. That's the part I'd argue actually matters — not that AI can generate things quickly, but that it can be built into infrastructure disciplined enough to trust with real client-facing production, at a scale one person could never sustain manually.

title: From a 131MB PDF to a Phone Scan: Turning Static Guest Booklets Into a Live Guide
summary: Soroi Collection's guest information lived in scanned, print-oriented PDFs the size of a movie file. I rebuilt it as a single-page site per property, scannable by QR, that shows guests today's actual weather and tonight's actual moon phase.

links.label: Soroi Blue Diani guide (static copy, widgets not yet live)

bodyHtml:
The problem

Before this, "guest information" at Soroi Collection's lodges meant a printed booklet — the kind of thing you find on the desk in every hotel room, run off in bulk and reprinted whenever anything changed. The actual files behind that print run are still sitting in the project: a 60MB all-in-one PDF for Samburu Lodge, a 131MB "Guest Welcome" PDF for Amboseli. These aren't lightweight one-pagers — they're large, print-native documents, built to be laid out on paper and handed over at check-in, not opened on a phone.

That format has real costs beyond the printing itself. Every update — a Wi-Fi password change, a new activity, a corrected phone number — means a reprint, and the version in the room is only ever as current as the last print run. And because it's built for paper, it can only ever say what was true when it was printed: today's weather, tonight's moon, the current exchange rate all have to be left out entirely, or printed as a vague range that's wrong half the time (a wall calendar can't tell you it's a full moon tonight).

What I did

I rebuilt the guest guide as what it actually needed to be: a page, not a document. Each property gets a single, self-contained HTML site — no app, no login, no backend — opened by scanning a QR code in the room. It's built mobile-first: one continuous scroll, section by section (welcome, your room, dining, the pool, activities, services, reference), with the same brand fonts and per-property color system used across Soroi's printed collateral, so it doesn't feel like a bolted-on afterthought next to the physical brand.

Two properties are live with this rebuild so far — Amboseli and Samburu Lodge — and it's from here that the interesting part of the brief starts: once the information is a live web page instead of a printed page, it can actually know things.

Live weather, not a printed range. Both live guides call a live weather API on page load and render today's actual temperature, conditions, and sunrise/sunset for that property's exact coordinates — with a plain-language fallback ("Conditions unavailable — check with reception") if the request fails, rather than a broken widget.

Tonight's actual moon phase, calculated, not fetched. This one doesn't call an API at all — moon phase is fully predictable from the date, so it's computed client-side from the calendar math (days since a known new moon, divided by the ~29.53-day lunar cycle), rendered against a set of eight custom phase icons. No dependency, no key, no network call that can fail.

Live currency conversion, the same pattern again — a live exchange-rate fetch converts USD and EUR to Kenyan shillings on the spot, with the same honest fallback if the rate service is unreachable, so a guest checking "what's a dollar worth today" gets today's actual number instead of a printed rate that's stale within a week of the booklet going to print.

The throughline across all three of these is the same design decision: wherever the printed version had to either omit time-sensitive information or print something that goes stale, the digital version either fetches it live or calculates it — and every one of them fails gracefully to a plain message instead of a broken interface, because a guest on lodge Wi-Fi at dawn shouldn't see a stack trace instead of a weather icon.

The result

  • Two properties (Amboseli, Samburu Lodge) now run a live, mobile-first digital guest guide, replacing print files that ran from 60 to 131MB.
  • Guests get today's real weather, tonight's real moon phase, and a live currency conversion on the same page they'd otherwise have flipped past in a printed booklet — none of which is possible in a static document.
  • An update to any section — a price, a Wi-Fi password, an activity time — is a text edit to one file, not a reprint.
  • Samburu Lodge's guide is the only one currently under real version control with a working history of iterative fixes (mobile layout, accessibility on the Wi-Fi section, map legibility) — the kind of continuous small correction a printed booklet can't get without a whole new print run.

Open honestly, not yet finished: Soroi Blue Diani has the same single-page guide format but not yet the weather, moon, or currency widgets — it's running on static copy for now. And "live location" isn't actually built anywhere yet: GPS coordinates are shown as plain text (the same coordinates that feed the weather lookup), and property wayfinding is a static map image, not an interactive or distance-aware one. If a "live location" feature is part of the story you want to tell, it's the one honest gap between what's built and what's planned — worth flagging before it goes in a public case study as fact.
